title: A Black Hole Caught Shredding a White Dwarf
hook: The Einstein Probe may have caught a long-sought 'missing link' black hole tearing apart a dense white dwarf star — and devouring it in a burst of X-ray flashes.
key_points: Astronomers think they saw an intermediate-mass black hole rip apart a white dwarf.
Such mid-sized black holes are a long-sought 'missing link' between small and giant ones.
Shredding a star by tides like this is called a tidal disruption event.
The Einstein Probe caught it early as intense X-ray flashes unlike a normal gamma-ray burst.
content_html: According to a ScienceDaily report, astronomers may have witnessed one of the rarest cosmic events on record: an intermediate-mass black hole ripping apart a dense white dwarf star and swallowing it. Intermediate-mass black holes — bigger than the ones left by dying stars, but far smaller than the giants at the hearts of galaxies — are a long-sought "missing link," so catching one in action would be a notable find.
extra_html: When a star wanders too close to a black hole, the hole's gravity pulls much harder on the near side than the far side, stretching and tearing the star apart. Astronomers call this a tidal disruption event. The Einstein Probe space telescope reportedly caught this one in its earliest moments, recording an unusual sequence of intense X-ray flashes that did not look like a typical gamma-ray burst. If confirmed, the event would offer a rare look at both an elusive class of black hole and the violent physics of a star being torn apart.
